earlier_scan.note: Only discourse study (Hodder 1999) and texts for Mayoyao Ifugao; no phonology/stress description located

new_statements.quote: Hodder 1999: '... Geminate glottal stops are written '-, as in hu'-ud 'spear'. Stress is phonemic but is not written.' Lambrecht 1932: '[the] accent denotes the syllable on which the stress is laid. It is sometimes very difficult to determine this, especially for words of two syllables, for sometimes the stress seems to be laid on the first syllable, sometimes on the second of the same word. Therefore one must not wonder if in our texts the same word ...'

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files checked in (1) The named file contains both quoted passages exactly as reported. I re-queried the Google Books GData feed independently (2026-09-17) and both snippets reproduced verbatim from the volumes themselves: PJL 30 (1999, id RChZAAAAMAAJ) '... Geminate glottal stops are written ' -, as in hu ' - ud ' spear '. Stress is phonemic but is not written. 5 Some verb affixes indicate the semantic role of S and P...' (preceded in the same footnote by 'Mayoyao Ifugao is spoken by the people of the Mayoyao and Aguinaldo districts of Ifugao province... consonants and 5 vowels...'); and Mayawyaw Ritual 1 (1932, ids kVi-PBBS5FAC, Uo0ZU3bAc84C, vQG1AAAAIAAJ, OZ4RAAAAIAAJ, iTceoKSgu54C) '...…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Mayoyao Ifugao is contrastive (lexically specified, not predictable by position) and is not represented in the practical orthography; Lambrecht's Mayawyaw texts accordingly mark the stressed syllable word by word and he notes that in disyllables stress may be heard on either syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Lambrecht 1957 (Folklore Studies 16: 107 fn.1, Mayawyaw texts) marks a secondary stress with an accent above the vowel: it precedes the primary stress in reduplicated words, but follows it when enclitic personal pronouns (cha-á, cha-amí, chita-ú, cha-ayú, chichá) or a place/time demonstrative are attached to a vowel-final word. Hodder 1999 snippet says nothing about secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None in the accessible text. Lambrecht 1932 remarks that stress in two-syllable words is hard to determine and that the same word may appear accented differently in his texts.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical stress; Hodder's statement concerns the phonemic system and the SIL practical orthography (stress unwritten). Lambrecht's remarks concern citation/text forms in his Mayawyaw transcriptions; his 1960 Lagawe (Tuwali) hudhud study adds that chant metre can shift stress relative to ordinary speech (not Mayoyao).
new_statements.identity_note: Hodder 1999 describes Mayoyao Ifugao as spoken in Mayoyao and Aguinaldo municipalities, Ifugao Province (= mayo1262). Lambrecht's 'Mayawyaw' (Mayawyaw Ritual 1932-41; Mayawyaw tales in Folklore Studies 16, 1957; Ifugaw-English Dictionary 1978) is the same variety (Mayawyaw = Mayoyao). Excluded as not this language: Lambrecht 1960 Ifugaw Hu'dhud (Lagawe text = Tuwali Ifugao, tuwa1243), Lambrecht 1955 Ifugao Tales (Kiangan = tuwa1243), Conklin 1991 (Bayninan/Banaue = Amganad/Tuwali area), and Zorc 1978/1993 'Ifugao/Ifg' (= Batad Ifugao, bata1298, from Newell 1968).

sources.citation: Conklin, Harold C. 1991. A systematic orthography for writing Ifugao. Philippine Journal of Linguistics 22(1-2): 31-36. (archive.org rosettaproject_ifk_ortho-1) -- Bayninan/Banaue Ifugao
sources.note: Vowels 'in prefinal syllables... may occur in long (V̄) as well as in short, unmarked (V) form'; length marked with macron; no statement about stress; claims the 20-sign system suffices for all Ifugao dialects.

sources.citation: Lambrecht, Francis. 1957. Ifugaw tales: Banawe and Mayawyaw. Folklore Studies 16: 107-184. (open access, asianethnology.org)
sources.note: p.107 fn.1 (phonetic key referred to Mayawyaw Ritual 1, pp. 22-23): 'After a vowel the acute accent denotes the syllable on which the stress is laid. Above a vowel the acute accent denotes the syllable on which the secondary stress is laid. The latter (a) precedes the former in reduplicated words, but (b) follows if the personal pronouns cha-á, cha-amí, chita-ú, cha-ayú and chichá are enclitic, or if a demonstrative of place or time is joined to a word that ends with a vowel'. Stress is marked word by word in the Mayawyaw texts; no placement rule stated.
